title: Design, prototyping and handoff with Claude Design

items.scenario: A designer finishes a three-screen flow in Claude Design. The developer picking up the ticket asks for 'screenshots in Jira so I can build it'.
items.question: What is the best handoff?
options: Export high-resolution PNGs of each screen and attach them to the ticket
Export a PDF of the flow so the developer has a fixed reference to build against
Record a short screen-capture video walking through the prototype
Send the design to Claude Code and attach a handoff note listing open decisions
items.explanation: Handing over the design lets the coding agent continue from its structure (components, tokens, copy) instead of reverse-engineering pixels. The handoff note covers what no design carries.
distractors: Pixels lose components, tokens and states, so the developer has to infer them and drift creeps in.
A PDF flattens structure just as a screenshot does, plus it loses the interaction.
Video shows behaviour but carries no structure, tokens or copy to build from.

items.scenario: Pre-sales has a clickable mobile concept prototype. The client's product lead wants to tap through it on their phone before Thursday's pitch.
items.question: Which output fits what the recipient will do?
options: A PDF export, because it's easy to attach to an email and opens on any phone
A hosted or standalone HTML version they can open and click through
A PPTX export so it can be added to the pitch deck
A .zip of the source files so they have everything
items.explanation: Choose the export by what the recipient will do next. Clicking through on a phone needs the interaction to survive, which HTML or a hosted send preserves.
distractors: A PDF flattens the prototype, so the interaction they want to try is lost.
Slides suit presenting, not tapping through a flow on a phone.
Source files are for storage or further work, not for a stakeholder to experience the flow.

items.scenario: You start a client's internal tool mock-up by typing 'design a dashboard for the ops team' and get something generic. Three rounds of 'make it more modern' haven't helped.
items.question: What is the most effective next move?
options: Switch to a different artifact type and start again with the same request
Keep iterating with more descriptive adjectives until the result finally looks right to you
Write a brief (audience, platform, task, constraints, brand), then request specific changes
Ask Claude to generate ten variations, then pick the best-looking one for the client
items.explanation: Claude fills every gap in the brief with a guess. A brief that sets audience, platform, task, constraints and brand, followed by specific testable feedback, converges; adjectives don't.
distractors: The type isn't the problem; the missing brief is.
Untestable feedback produces endless rounds without convergence.
More variations of an unspecified design still guess at audience and constraints.

items.scenario: During an accessibility review, Claude looks at a screenshot and says the grey helper text 'appears to meet the 4.5:1 contrast requirement'. The release is tomorrow.
items.question: What should you do before accepting this?
options: Compute the contrast ratio from the actual colour tokens with a contrast checker
Accept it, since Claude analysed the full-resolution image and stated the ratio
Ask Claude to look again more carefully and confirm its answer
Increase the font size slightly so that the stricter normal-text requirement no longer applies
items.explanation: Vision estimates are approximate, and for contrast near a threshold approximately right is wrong. Measure on the real token values; a computed 4.4:1 fails.
distractors: Resolution doesn't make a visual estimate of a ratio exact; small colour differences decide pass or fail.
A second look is still an estimate, not a measurement.
A slight increase may not reach the large-text size, and it dodges checking whether the colour is compliant.

items.scenario: Your team is about to start a client's screen set. The client has a design system, but nobody is sure whether the version on a shared drive or the one in the main code repository is current.
items.question: What should you do before importing?
options: Import the shared-drive version, since the designers maintain and update that copy
Import both and let Claude merge them into one system
Skip the design system and apply the brand by hand later
Confirm with the design-system owner which source is canonical, then import it
items.explanation: Design-system location and ownership is a governance question. Importing a stale copy makes it the house style by accident; the owner decides what is canonical.
distractors: Assuming which copy is current is how a stale system gets adopted.
Merging two possibly conflicting systems creates a third, unowned one.
Re-skinning every screen later is slower and lets tokens drift.

items.scenario: A developer built a screen from a handed-off design. In QA, the loading, empty and API-error states look improvised and inconsistent with the rest of the app.
items.question: What would have prevented this?
options: Exporting the design at a higher resolution so details were visible
A handoff note listing which states were designed and what engineering still had to decide
Asking the developer to copy the default state's styling for every other state they need
Running the heuristic evaluation after the code was merged
items.explanation: Undesigned states don't survive a handoff because they were never in the design. The handoff note makes them explicit so they get designed or decided, not invented.
distractors: Resolution can't show states that were never designed.
That produces states that look the same but don't communicate loading, emptiness or failure.
Reviewing after merge finds the problem late instead of preventing it.

items.scenario: A heuristic review of a logistics screen finds a destructive 'Cancel shipment' button styled exactly like 'Save' and placed beside it.
items.question: Which fix best addresses the underlying usability principle?
options: Add a tooltip to the cancel button explaining what it does and that it discards changes
Move both buttons to the bottom of the page
Make the destructive action visually distinct, separate it from Save, and confirm it
Rename the button to 'Cancel' so the label is shorter
items.explanation: This is error prevention: a destructive action that looks and sits like a routine one invites mistakes. Visual distinction, separation and confirmation prevent the slip.
distractors: A tooltip needs hovering and does nothing for the user who clicks by mistake.
Moving both keeps the identical styling and adjacency that cause the error.
A shorter label makes the action more ambiguous, not safer.

items.scenario: A stakeholder review is scheduled on an AI-powered prototype artifact you built. Twelve people from the client will open it during the session.
items.question: What should you tell them beforehand?
options: That AI features in the prototype run on each viewer's own account and usage
That they need your login to see the AI features
That the prototype must be exported to PDF before anyone outside the team can review it
Nothing, because shared artifacts use only the creator's usage
items.explanation: AI-powered artifacts run on the viewer's own account, so each reviewer's usage is consumed and their access applies. Say so before the review, not during it.
distractors: Sharing credentials breaks policy, and the artifact doesn't work that way.
A PDF would remove the interaction the review is meant to test.
That's backwards; the viewer's account and usage are what get used.

items.scenario: A front-end lead says: 'The design file is the spec, so if it's not in the design, the developer should just follow existing code patterns.' The design covers six screens at one breakpoint.
items.question: What is the strongest response?
options: Agree, since following existing code patterns will keep the implementation consistent with the app
Ask the designer to add every breakpoint and state before any code is written
Ask Claude Code to infer the missing decisions from the design while it builds the screens
List what the design can't carry (data, states, breakpoints, errors) and give each an owner
items.explanation: A design carries layout, components, tokens and copy; it doesn't carry data contracts, state, undesigned breakpoints or error logic. Making those explicit, with owners, is what prevents silent invention.
distractors: Existing patterns may not fit, and the decisions still get made silently by whoever codes them.
Designing everything up front delays delivery; some decisions belong to engineering, not design.
Inference is exactly the invention the handoff note exists to prevent.

items.scenario: Two weeks before a hard deadline, you learn that a client's design system lives only on a hosted design site that the vendor has announced it is closing on a fixed date.
items.question: How should you handle this on the engagement?
options: Keep working as normal and migrate the design system after the current deliverable ships
Export screenshots of the design system pages as a backup
Log it as a dated risk with an owner, migrate early, and verify against a known screen
Rebuild the design system from scratch inside your own tooling
items.explanation: A dated platform change is a delivery risk: record it, assign the owner, migrate before the date, and verify the migrated system reproduces a known screen.
distractors: If the site closes mid-deliverable, the house style becomes unavailable when you need it most.
Screenshots lose the tokens and components that make a design system usable.
Rebuilding from scratch is slower and risks drifting from the canonical system.
